title: The abbot (ch. 2)
hook: the abbot holds the place of Christ and must adapt to each person

segments.voice: Yesterday, a school for beginners: Benedict hoped to set down nothing harsh or heavy. Your line was nothing harsh. When you stalled at something new, how did you talk to yourself? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

Should a good boss treat everyone the same? It sounds like fairness. Same rules, same tone, same speech for the whole team. But a coach who barks at every player the same way loses some of them. One needs a push. One needs a joke. One needs to be left alone until Thursday. Saint Benedict's Rule has a chapter on the person in charge of the monastery, and it asks something harder than sameness. Today's word: abbot.
screen: `TREAT EVERYONE THE SAME?` → `ONE NEEDS A PUSH, ONE A JOKE.` → `THE PERSON IN CHARGE.`

segments.voice: The second chapter of the Rule starts high. It says the abbot is believed to hold the place of Christ in the monastery, because he's called by Christ's own name for the Father: abba. Benedict points to Paul, who says in the Douay-Rheims that we have received a spirit "whereby we cry: Abba (Father)." So abbot, in the Rule's own words, is a father's name. Then the chapter turns the weight around. Because he holds that place, the abbot will answer to God for every soul in his care. He's to teach more by what he does than by what he says. He's not to put a monk born free ahead of one who came from slavery. And then the line that gives today's carry. The abbot, Benedict says, has to fit himself to each person: their character, their understanding. Coax one. Correct another. Reason with a third. Some respond to a gentle word, others need it said plainly. The Rule says he should serve many different temperaments, and adapt himself so that none of the flock is lost. Notice what Benedict isn't saying. He doesn't say the rules change for favorites. He says the same care has to wear different clothes for different people. Every monk gets the abbot's full attention. Not every monk gets the same speech. It's a hard job, and the Rule knows it. It calls the role a difficult and demanding work: ruling souls. A father's name, a heavy account, and a habit of looking at each face before speaking.
screen: `A FATHER'S NAME: ABBA.` · `HE ANSWERS FOR EVERY SOUL.` · `COAX, CORRECT, REASON.` · `SAME CARE, DIFFERENT CLOTHES.` · then, large: `WHEREBY WE CRY: ABBA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: adapt to someone's needs. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two people you look after, or work with, or live with. Picture them side by side. Ask what each one needs from you right now. Maybe one needs a push, and the other needs you to go gently. Maybe one needs more words, and the other fewer. Don't decide anything big. Just let their two faces be different. If you pray, you can ask God for the wisdom to care for each of them as they are. The bell holds the time.
Abbot. The father of a monastery, named, the Rule says, from abba, who holds the place of Christ and must fit himself to each person in his care. Today's word.
Your line: each one differently. Today, with one person, ask what they need before you give what you usually give. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: In Benedictine monasteries the monks elect their abbot or abbess, who leads the community and is responsible for each member's care, following chapter 2 of the Rule.

myth: the Rule tells the abbot to treat every monk exactly alike
it tells him to fit himself to each person's character and understanding.
the Rule links the abbot's name to abba, father
pointing to Paul: whereby we cry, Abba (Father).
the abbot may put freeborn monks ahead of the rest
the Rule says he's not to put a monk born free ahead of one who came from slavery.

fork.setup: you're the abbot. one monk needs a firm word, another is easily crushed. what does the Rule ask of you?
options: give both the same firm speech.
fit yourself to each: correct one, coax the other.
fork.reveal: the Rule asks the abbot to adapt to each temperament, so that none of the flock is lost.

original.note: an Aramaic word for father, kept in the Greek of Romans 8:15; the Rule gives it as the abbot's name.

trapdoor: what you thought: an abbot is the boss of a monastery.
what it means: a father who holds the place of Christ and fits his care to each person.
what a scholar hears: Rule ch. 2 grounds the title in Romans 8:15, Abba, Pater, and warns the abbot he will give account for every soul.

notes: Chapter 2 is paraphrased (Gasquet 1909 wording unverified). Points to confirm: 'Christi enim agere vices in monasterio creditur' with the appeal to Romans 8:15; teaching more by deeds than words; no favoritism for birth or wealth; adapting to 'multorum servire moribus'; 'rem difficilem et arduam, regere animas'; giving account for every soul.
The abbot/abba link is given as the Rule's own words, not as an independent etymology.
Greek of Romans 8:15 has 'Αββα ὁ πατήρ'; the original game shows ἀββα (breathing mark, no accent); editions vary (Αββα, ἀββά). Keeper to confirm.
howItsDone mentions abbesses and election (ch. 64); confirm.

Editor pass: 'not to love one monk more because of family or wealth' corrected to the Rule's actual contrast (ch. 2: 'non praeponatur ingenuus ex servitio convertenti', freeborn vs one from slavery), in voice and myth; hook's 'loses half of them' (a number) changed to 'some'.
